# Discussion {#sec-discussion .deo-discussion}

Across the eight cases, citizens held leading roles at every stage only where
the group that founded the initiative kept contributing to the work, as in the
Patient-Led Research Collaborative and LaporCovid-19. In the institution-led
cases, citizen involvement was mostly instrumental, limited to tasks that the
lead institution had already defined, such as data collection or consultation
on selected components. In the two failures, the people whose data were used had
no research role at all. This is consistent with the systematic review of
mental-health citizen science, in which citizens contributed mostly through data
collection [@todowede2023]. Citizen leadership was rare in these cases. Where it
occurred, it shaped the research question and produced evidence before official
or conventional sources did.

Citizen involvement changed the research more readily than it changed
decisions. In the sources we reviewed, documented use of findings by
decision-makers was scarce, even in the two founder-led cases. LaporCovid-19's
advocacy contributed to the withdrawal of a self-funded vaccination plan, but
its data challenged official figures [@laporcovid2021]. Findings from the
Patient-Led Research Collaborative drew attention, but we found no documented
route into decisions. The only case with documented use was the Indonesian Red
Cross community-based surveillance, whose alerts were fed into the national
early-warning system [@ifrc2021]. Its volunteers, however, only reported to a
protocol designed by others. These cases suggest a trade-off, where working
inside government systems kept citizens at the reporting stage, while
independent leadership by the founding group left its relationship with
government contested. No case clearly combined citizen leadership with
documented use of findings. The three conditions below are synthesized from the
cases and have not been tested. They bear on a practical problem: how can
citizen leadership over the research question be combined with the
institutional routes through which findings become policy or programmes?

The first condition is a pathway from findings to decisions, agreed at the
design stage with a named institutional collaborator. In the Red Cross case,
the citizen-contributed alerts were fed into the national early-warning system,
and local governments took ownership to resolve the issue [@ifrc2021]. On the
other hand, CoAct produced 14 recommendations and public commitments from a
city councillor and the director of the National Mental Health Pact
[@ub2022assembly; @bcn2023plan]. We could trace no adoption, which suggests
that commitments need to be recorded and followed up. In LaporCovid-19, the
health-worker database was built with professional associations, a news
organisation and a research unit, and the analysis had Ministry of Health
ethics approval [@ekawati2022]. This is a single observation, but it shows that
a civil-society database can gain institutional standing without being run by
an institution. Wider evidence points the same way, with caution. A systematic
review of 145 studies found that collaboration and relationships between
researchers and policymakers were among the most often reported facilitators of
evidence use [@oliver2014]. Poor access to relevant research, and research
arriving too late, were the main barriers. A scoping review of integrated
knowledge translation, in which research is done in partnership with
decision-makers from the outset, found that most evaluated partnerships
reported at least one positive outcome [@gagliardi2016]. It is not known which
partnership strategies lead to which outcomes. A benchmark outside our eight
cases is the NIH RECOVER programme on Long COVID. Its adult-cohort protocol
states that patient representatives give input on all study processes, and some
were recruited from advocacy groups including the Patient-Led Research
Collaborative [@horwitz2023]. Representatives have described the partnership
from their side [@kim2023]. A survey of RECOVER's clinical-trial protocol
working groups found that most patient, caregiver and community representatives
felt their input was valued, but gaps in role clarity, communication and
integration of feedback persisted [@leverty2026]. Embedding patients in a
research programme is not the same as institutions using findings that patients
generated (item C3). A news feature in *Nature* reported that the survey had
been mentioned in some 60 policy statements [@fairbank2024]. Overall, the
benchmark suggests that influence on research design and on policy discussion
is achievable, while decision-makers' use of findings is harder to show.

The second condition is legitimacy, and both failures broke down at consent. In
the Crisis Text Line case, data given in crisis under a terms-of-service link
were later licensed for a commercial purpose [@eysenbach2025]. In Samaritans
Radar, people were monitored without knowing it, under an opt-out design
[@responsibledata_radar]. Both activities were discredited and ended under
public pressure. A similar loss of public trust ended England's national plan
to share general-practice records. That plan proceeded without what has been
called a "social licence" [@carter2015]. Positive approaches exist. The
MindKind study asked young people in India, South Africa and the United Kingdom
how their mental-health data should be governed [@mindkind2022]. It found that
they held strong preferences about who should access their data. They were also
willing to help design more open data-sharing arrangements. In Indonesia,
personal data protection is regulated by Law 27/2022 [@uupdp2022], and the
Health Law of 2023 contains provisions on health information systems
[@uu17_2023]. Although we do not analyse their provisions here, these cases
suggest that consent for mental-health data should be specific to each study
and recorded so that it can be checked. It should be renewed when the purpose
changes, and opt-in by default. These requirements are developed as principles
in Paper 2 of this series.

The third condition is credibility, which depends on being able to see how a
project was run. Most of the consistently lacking items were unreported rather
than shown to be absent. From public sources, therefore, we cannot tell whether
a project omitted a practice or simply did not write about it. The same gap was
found in the mental-health citizen science literature [@todowede2023]. Reporting
guidance already exists. The GRIPP2 checklists describe how to report patient
and public involvement [@staniszewska2017]. The systematic review proposed
mental-health-specific reporting recommendations for each ECSA principle
[@todowede2023]. Our 18 items could serve as a complementary checklist, allowing
projects to state explicitly which practices they followed, including whether
they evaluated themselves. Reporting also needs to say whose experience is
represented. Typologies of participation, from Arnstein's ladder [@arnstein1969]
to Haklay's levels [@haklay2013], rank projects by how much power citizens hold.
They do not distinguish which citizens hold it. In LaporCovid-19, the leading
roles were held by a coalition of experts, journalists and activists, while lay
members of the public mainly reported data [@rinaldi2024; @ekawati2022]. The
Patient-Led Research Collaborative was led by people with Long COVID who
describe themselves as patient-researchers [@mccorkell2021; @fitzgerald2024].
Participation dominated by a small or well-connected group risks the "elite
capture" described in lived-experience research [@okoroji2023]. The people most
affected by distress, who may have the least time, energy and confidence to take
part, remain unheard. Future frameworks should record not only the level of
participation but also whose experience is represented at each level.

## Recommendations for future research and practice

Drawing on the reviewed cases, we propose a design sequence for citizen-centred
research on stress, depression, anxiety, burnout and resilience. The sequence
begins with citizens helping to formulate and sharpen the research question, so
that the study addresses what matters to the people affected. In the two
founder-led cases, this produced evidence that official or conventional sources
had not, such as the health-worker deaths that no official source was counting
[@ekawati2022]. In the two failures, by contrast, organisations acted on behalf
of people in distress without asking them. In a nine-country study, Indonesian
respondents identified community support, including mental support, as a way they
wanted to contribute [@tan2024]. Before data collection, projects should obtain
opt-in, study-specific consent. Where feasible, they should also agree with a
named institutional counterpart how the findings might be used. Results should
then be returned to participants in a usable form. The study should be evaluated
and reported against the 18 items, so that readers can judge how it was run and
whose experience it represents. Indonesia has a channel to build on in lay
mental health cadres. Evaluations of their training, however, have not measured
outcomes for patients or communities, and support for volunteers appears uneven
[@susanti2024; @sitorukmi2025]. Within this series, Paper 2 develops the consent
and reporting lessons into principles for research-ready health data. Paper 3
assesses an open-source research platform against those principles. Paper 4 is a
baseline study of depression, anxiety, burnout, resilience and functioning among
adults in three Indonesian cities. Beyond the series, the scoring framework
needs validation, and interviews with project teams could show whether
unreported practices took place. A pilot mental-health study in Indonesia, with
a pre-agreed pathway to a named institution, would test whether the sequence
makes findings actionable.

## Strengths and limitations

The main limitation of this study is its reliance on public documents. Practices
that were not reported could not be scored, so the many `NR` scores more likely
reflect gaps in reporting than gaps in practice. The cases were selected
purposively and are not representative of citizen science in mental health, so
the patterns described here should be read as hypotheses and not as frequencies.
Several cases also rested on organisational reports, project websites or news
coverage, which may present projects favourably or selectively. This applies in
particular to the D1 score for LaporCovid-19, which rests on organisational
sources. That score was revised from not reported to partly met after a
follow-up search on 16 November 2026. The scoring framework is new and has not
been validated beyond this review, and agreement between coders is reported only
as a percentage of cells agreed. Defining the unit of analysis and who counts as
a citizen also required judgement, particularly for the failure cases, in which
the people whose data were used had no research role. In addition, the lead
author founded a company that develops a research platform evaluated later in
this series; the steps taken to limit bias are described in the Methods and
Declarations. Finally, we found no Indonesian citizen science project focused on
mental health. This may reflect a true absence or the limits of our search, and
the Indonesian recommendations therefore draw on benchmarks from other fields
and countries.

Notwithstanding these limitations, the review has several merits. All cases were
scored by two coders on a common framework, with rules fixed before scoring.
Failure cases were included and scored on the same terms as successes, which
limits the tendency to describe only what worked. The review also adds evidence
from a middle-income country, addressing a gap in the existing literature
[@todowede2023].
